## The question

Study time is one of the few influences on grades that students, families, and schools can actually change, while factors like past failures or family background are largely fixed. Knowing how much study time is associated with grades, compared with those fixed factors, helps school counselors, teachers, and families decide whether encouraging study habits is worth the effort. Our question is: among students in a Portuguese-language secondary course, how is weekly study time associated with the final grade, after accounting for past class failures and absences?

We use the Student Performance dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (Cortez, 2008), where each row is one student in the Portuguese-language course at one of two secondary schools in Portugal (649 students). The response is the final grade (G3), a score from 0 to 20. The main predictors are weekly study time, past class failures, and absences, and we also consider other background and behavior variables such as alcohol use, parents' education, and plans for higher education. We deliberately leave out the first- and second-period grades because they are nearly the same measurement as the final grade and would hide the role of things schools can act on. One important limitation is that study time is self-reported in four broad bands rather than hours, so our results describe patterns across groups of students at these two schools, not precise effects or individual students.
